notes.note:
# 
Um, so 1st is how you were thinking about your career back in high school and then what, um, sort of pushed you to take engineering in college, uh, were you totally into it? Was their parent pressure? How did that work out? And then obviously after college, you would have again had thoughts as to what you want to do. So what you got into right after college. And then finally, I want to move into how you gone into trading, what you like about it, what are the skills you need to be a good trader? How did you develop those skills? What advice would you give to 13, 14, 15 year olds today? That might have an interest in financial markets that might have an interest in in, you know, trading, how can they go about developing those skills? Not only academic, but even non-academic, there's a whole range of behavioural traits that good traders have. How can you go about developing those? I know you do a lot of meditation. How does that help? Would you say that meditation will also sort of help people in other pursuits apart from trading? And finally, I will, we should finish with what your idea of a good high school education looks like, what you would want as an adult, as a person who's lived 40 years. What would you tell our 8th and ninth graders to focus on so that they're well prepared and ready for the future?

1. 1. I was preparing for IIT but simply cause everyone wanted to get into IIT. Was a pretty good student, actually a topper or amongst the toppers in school by a fair margin. By second year however my interest towards pure science became more pronounced and I ended up getting a lot more interested in the research aspect of things. Physics was something I loved and was looking at studying nuclear physics. However due to a lack of understanding about career other after doing pure physics was led to doing engineering. Finally I became disillusioned and just started exploring all the different paths and then somehow landed up at RVCE to do my engineering. Idea was to do some graduation till I figured out what I really wanted to do in life
   2. Immediately after college the world was facing the global financial crisis and several of my classmates had their offers rescinded. I was Lucky however as I was able to get a job immediately and in a pretty interesting company. So I landed in the job immediately after. I really did not like the fact that we were just doing some data cookie work for the “thinkers” who were sitting in the US. My manager once commented that I did not need to learn or understand the GLM model but just run it and share the outcome or the results so that the guy in US could analyse it. She was a phd or something and from a decent college. I hated it, why would I work like a coolie and was this all that we were good at? A little later I realised this was the kind of work that was sent to India mostly. I was determined to not take up a career path and do something different. Something which made me feel more valued or rather something where I really was setting the agenda rather than being a day clerk. Even though there were IIT’ians and people from IIM who took pride in this work I did not. I was ambitious and perhaps a little too ambitious
   3. After graduating and these jobs I decided that if I did MBA I would get more meaningful work. The result was me writing several entrance exams for MBA colleges within a couple of months of leaving my job. Mind you between my first and second job there was a gap where I did try to work on something called prefab structures which was interesting and also treatment plants for hospitals which would treat the waste output from hospitals before releasing them in city sewage. That’s a story for another time though. So after quitting my second job and writing my entrance exams I had som time on hand. That was also the time when my brother had taken a franchise for a stock broking firm and I decided to give it a go. The other buisiness was trading in garments and textiles whic was hardly interesting. Also there wasn’t much scope in that. So I got into stock broking and suddenly found myself doing analysis. I was supposed to get customers and help them trade but a major part of that was advising them. You cannot advise if you don’t know much. So I started analysing them myself since I soon learnt that the parent company which had given us franchise was giving us rubbish research. My first year was tough, very tough. It was 16 hours a day and no breaks. I just managed to sleep between work and did nothing else. Almost every waking hour was devoted to markets.
   4. That intense year built my understanding of the markets and put me in a strong position. I lacked coding skills that someone may have had but I developed great market sense. I did not need to write a long piece of code to understand what the market was doing but instead just started to read it a lot better. A lot of the strategies I just learnt on my own. But the one thing that really helped me was getting the best books on technical analysis that I could find and read them and apply them in the real world. I never settled for anything else. The best book and author it always was. By a lot of trial and error I stayed realising what did not work, and let me tell you almost nothing worked. But it gave me a foundational knowledge on which I with the dint of my hard work and thinking was able to build a framework for successful trading 
   5. I am successful in trading across a large segment of markets except for perhaps the options which are a separate area of expertise in themselves. Success doesn’t mean Ferrari though, it mean being able to generate consistent profits which enable you to meet your expenses and have a generally good life. Maybe Mercedes is waiting in the future but not there yet. 
   6. If you are interested in financial markets my suggestion is to get down to actually “doing” something. Just reading about things will never teach you much. Till you learn and experience the pain of losing money or the pressure of making money for your clients all the strategies and learnings are just theoretical. Get down to actually tracking  financial news and read a lot of wires. Try and do paper trades or deep dive into a company and predict the actual earnings. Try and focus on actually reading the quarterly market reports. Anyone can do that using an AI tool nowadays. So you like video games? Great, try to read up about the company that made it and if it’s profitable, what’s the future like for them. Find something relatable. Back it up with reading and theory and see what do you really learn. The theory in the book versus the real thing out there, what’s the difference? How can you use your knowledge and apply it in the real world is what will set you apart and not just reading and “knowing” stuff. Finally read a lot ! You need to know a lot to be able to predict what the markets could possibly do. 
   7. Trading is like elite sports. You have to be extremely fit mentally and physically to be able to handle all the pressure and to process large amount of information in a short time. I feel my spiritual side helps me do that a lot better. Also intense pressure means I need to balance it out with breaks. I try to get a good sleep and workout regularly. Try and focus on my diet as well. This I feel is the cornerstone of being healthy and in a good mood so one can really tackle the challenge of the markets
   8. Meditation helps in all areas of life but that’s not something I want to talk much about. There are traders who perhaps don’t meditate but who am I to judge on that
   9. A good High school education should allow a child to really explore the concepts and understand the first principles. The basic concepts. Know them and then try to actually apply them in real life. Should expose to different areas of study so they can explore other interests. Most importantly develop independent thinking. Just cause someone says something doesn’t mean you swallow it without questioning. Question everything!! That doesn’t mean you have to be disrespectful but it means you ask questions when you don’t understand things. You will learn that as human beings we barely understand much at all. Look for evidence based approach when deciding on things. I always go back and see what would my returns look like if I followed a particular strategy, think it through and only then really go all in. Till then I just test. You need to develop this approach right from a young age.
